Read 2026-11-11: 'AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud'; customer responsibility 'will be determined by the AWS Cloud services that a customer selects', including 'using IAM tools to apply the appropriate permissions'. The page does not name credentials specifically; managing them is read as part of the customer's IAM duty.

Read 2026-11-11: 'applied by AWS in the event that an IAM user's credentials have been compromised or exposed publicly'; denies actions such as iam:CreateUser, iam:CreateAccessKey, iam:AttachUserPolicy, ec2:RunInstances; 'Do NOT remove this policy. Instead, please follow the instructions specified in the support case'.

sources.cite: AWS re:Post Knowledge Center: What do I do if I notice unauthorized activity in my AWS account?
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 (re:Post article): create an updated access key and deactivate the original ('Don't delete the original access key during this step'); deactivate users you didn't create; review CloudTrail event history for unsanctioned keys, policies and roles; 'check for all resources in all AWS Regions, even in Regions that you didn't launch resources'; 'Back up any resources you need for investigation before deleting them'; enable MFA on the root user. It names the V2 quarantine policy; the policy reference (read the same day) documents V3.

sources.cite: AWS. IAM User Guide: Security best practices in IAM
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: workloads should use 'temporary credentials with IAM roles'; 'AWS managed policies might not grant least-privilege permissions for your specific use cases because they are available for use by all AWS customers. As a result, we recommend that you reduce permissions further by defining customer managed policies that are specific to your use cases'; require MFA; protect root user credentials.

sources.cite: AWS. IAM User Guide: Managed policies and inline policies
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: an AWS managed policy is 'created and administered by AWS' and 'You cannot change the permissions defined in AWS managed policies'; customer managed policies you 'create ... for your specific use cases'.

brief.situation: Tuesday 08:10. An email from AWS: the access key of your IAM user ci-deploy was found in a public GitHub repository. AWS opened a support case and attached a quarantine policy to the user. Your company runs everything in us-east-2 (Ohio).
handover: ci-deploy is the user the build pipeline uses to deploy. It has the AWS managed policy AdministratorAccess, 'to save time'.
A developer pushed a config file with the key last night.
The account normally spends about $1,500 a month against a $2,000 budget.
howItWorks: Learner-paced: nothing moves until you act. Investigate, contain, fix, then run the next days.
The board shows identities and resources by Region; the meters show the unauthorized charges and the month's projected spend.
Before you run the next days you are asked who was responsible and what you changed. The debrief scores what you did.

source.note: The 24 unauthorized instances cost about $70 an hour, about $1,680 a day, as Cost Explorer shows in the scenario.
One day per step of the week.

respQ.title: Whose job was this?
respQ.context: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, who was responsible for keeping this key safe?

choices.label: We were: credentials and permissions are security in the cloud
choices.feedback: Right. AWS secures the infrastructure; the customer manages its users, keys and permissions. AWS helped here, but the key was ours to protect.

choices.label: AWS was: it runs the account, so it should have stopped the leak
choices.feedback: No. AWS secures the cloud itself; who has which key and permission is the customer's side of the model.

plan.question: Before you run the next days: who was responsible for this key, what did the key do, and what stops it happening again?

parts.label: Responsibility and scope
parts.criteria: States that credentials and IAM permissions are the customer's responsibility (security in the cloud); names what the key did from CloudTrail (a new admin user, instances in two unused Regions).
parts.modelAnswer: Keys and permissions are our side of the shared responsibility model. CloudTrail shows the key created support-admin with AdministratorAccess and launched 24 instances in two Regions we never use.

parts.label: Containment and least privilege
parts.criteria: Deactivates the leaked key and leaves the quarantine policy on; disables the attacker's user; terminates the instances (after snapshots); replaces AdministratorAccess with a customer managed policy limited to what the pipeline needs; root MFA.
parts.modelAnswer: Deactivate the key and keep the quarantine. Disable support-admin, which the quarantine does not cover. Snapshot and terminate the instances. Give the pipeline a customer managed policy with only what it deploys; an AWS managed policy is written for everyone and is broader than this job needs.

expertPath.text: CloudTrail for the key: a new admin user and 24 instances. Every Region: two you never use. The bill: about $70 an hour.
Deactivate the leaked key and leave the quarantine on; disable support-admin; snapshot and terminate the instances.
A customer managed policy for the pipeline and root MFA. The trade-off: the pipeline waits an hour for a narrower policy instead of getting its old rights back at once.

overrun.headline: Unauthorized charges ran on
overrun.body: The unknown instances kept running at about $70 an hour. Check every Region, even ones you never use, and stop what you did not launch.

pathOpen.headline: The attacker came back
pathOpen.body: AWS's quarantine covers only the leaked user. The attacker's own admin user, or the leaked key once the quarantine came off, was a way back in. CloudTrail shows what to close.

fixed.headline: Contained and locked down
fixed.body: You scoped the incident, closed every way in, kept the evidence and cut the pipeline down to what it needs. That is the expert path.

partly.headline: Contained, by a rougher route
partly.body: Check whether you looked at CloudTrail and every Region, whether the leaked key itself was deactivated, and whether the pipeline still has broad rights.

scoring.modelReasoning: Under the shared responsibility model AWS secures the infrastructure and the customer manages its own users, keys and permissions, so a leaked key is the customer's to fix, with AWS's help. Scope it with CloudTrail and a check of every Region: the key created its own admin user, which AWS's quarantine does not cover. Deactivate the leaked key, leave the quarantine policy on, disable the attacker's user, and snapshot then terminate what you did not launch. The deeper fix is least privilege: an AWS managed policy such as AdministratorAccess or PowerUserAccess is written for every customer, so a customer managed policy with only what the pipeline deploys limits what the next leaked key can do. Workloads on AWS can use roles with temporary credentials instead of keys at all.
